title: The bow drops (1.40–1.47)
hook: the last argument, the last verse of chapter one, and a warrior sitting down in the middle of the field

segments.voice: Yesterday, I see no good in killing my kin: Gandiva slipping from his hand, and Arjuna's case against the war, heard in full. Your line was the honest objection. Today, the end of chapter one.

Some people know this moment. Weeks of holding it together, every argument made, to themselves and to everyone else. Then, one ordinary afternoon, in a parking lot or a kitchen or an office bathroom, they just sit down. Not because they decided to. Because they can't stand up anymore. That's where chapter one of the Gita ends. Not with a battle, but with the warrior Krishna drove into the middle of the field sitting down in his chariot, his bow on the floor.
screen: `WEEKS OF HOLDING IT TOGETHER.` → `ONE AFTERNOON, THEY SIT DOWN.` → `THE BOW ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Arjuna's last arguments, in verses forty to forty-four, are about what a war like this destroys beyond the dead. When a family is wiped out, he says, its old ways die with it: the rites, the offerings to the ancestors, the order that held a society together. Chaos follows, and the generations after are lost. It's the argument of a man from his own time and world, and people read it differently today: some commentators hear real grief for everything a war erases, some hear a mind grabbing any argument it can find. Either way, it ends in a cry. Alas, he says, we're about to commit a great wrong, killing our own people out of greed for a kingdom. Then the line that's hardest to hear: it would be better for me if the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapons in hand, killed me in battle, unarmed and not fighting back. And Sanjaya, telling the blind king, describes what he sees. In Sanskrit: visrijya sasharam chapam shoka samvigna manasah. Casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind shaken with grief, Arjuna sinks down onto the seat of his chariot, there between the two armies. That's the end of chapter one. And here's the surprise. Every chapter of the Gita has a title calling it a yoga, a path. This one is Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despair. Despair, counted as a path. None of Krishna's teaching happens without this. The book begins because a man sat down and said, I can't.
screen: `WHAT A WAR ERASES.` · `BETTER IF THEY KILLED ME UNARMED.` · `HE CASTS ASIDE HIS BOW.` · `THE YOGA OF DESPAIR.` · then, large: `THE BOOK BEGINS WITH I CAN'T.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been carrying and fighting with for too long, and picture it as a bow, heavy in your hands, arrows on your back. Without deciding anything about tomorrow, set it down beside you, let your hands be empty, and sit, the way Arjuna sits in his chariot in the middle of everything. You don't have to fix anything yet; saying I can't, honestly, is the start of the book.
Vishada. Despair, dejection: the word that names chapter one, Arjuna Vishada Yoga. Arjuna casts aside his bow and arrows and sits down, his mind shaken with grief.
Your line: I can't. Tomorrow, Krishna answers him. That's chapter one, all done.

howItsDone: Chapter one of the Gita is traditionally titled Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despair; many readers and teachers treat Arjuna's collapse at 1.47 as the necessary starting point for the teaching that follows.

notes: 1.40–1.44 include Arjuna's argument about the corruption of women of the family and varnasankara (mixing of varnas), and ancestors falling without pinda offerings. The script summarizes this as 'the rites, the offerings to the ancestors, the order that held a society together' and does not spell out the women/varna content. A Keeper should decide whether to name it explicitly.
'Some commentators hear real grief... some hear a mind grabbing any argument' is the script's summary of differing readings. Confirm.
Chapter colophon titles vary slightly across editions (Arjuna Vishada Yoga is standard). Confirm.
Gita 1.47 in some editions is numbered 1.46. Confirm.
